The neighbourhood seemed composed of back lanes, ditches, and small gardens, and had the look of a rather sleepy retreat. Wemmick’s dwelling was a tiny wooden cottage among garden plots, with its upper edge shaped and painted to resemble a battery furnished with cannon.

‘All my own work,’ said Wemmick. ‘A pretty sight, isn’t it?’

I praised it warmly. I believe it was the smallest house I had ever beheld, with the oddest Gothic windows, most of them mere imitations, and a Gothic doorway scarcely large enough to enter.

‘You see, that’s a proper flagstaff,’ Wemmick said, ‘and every Sunday I fly a proper flag. Now watch this. Once I’ve passed over the bridge, I draw it up—like so—and stop all communication.’

The bridge consisted of a plank across a ditch some four feet wide and two feet deep. Yet it was delightful to observe his pride as he raised and secured it, smiling throughout with genuine enjoyment rather than from habit.

‘Every evening at nine, by Greenwich time,’ said Wemmick, ‘the gun goes off. There he stands, you see! And once you hear him speak, I fancy you’ll agree he’s a Stinger.’

This artillery piece stood in a fortress of its own, built of lattice-work. An ingenious little arrangement of tarpaulin, something like an umbrella, sheltered it from the weather.

‘And behind,’ Wemmick continued, ‘where you can’t see it, so it doesn’t spoil the notion of fortifications—for my principle is, if you take up an idea, work it out and maintain it—I don’t know if you agree—’

I told him I agreed entirely.

‘—Behind, I keep a pig, with poultry and rabbits; and then I put together a little frame myself, you see, and raise cucumbers. At supper you can judge the sort of salad I grow. So, sir,’ said Wemmick, smiling once more, though with seriousness too, and shaking his head, ‘if you imagine the little place under siege, it could last a devilish long while where provisions are concerned.’

He next led me to a bower only a dozen yards distant, reached by a path of such cunning turns that the journey occupied a surprising time. Our glasses were already laid out in this retreat. The punch was cooling in an ornamental lake, beside which the bower stood. This round expanse of water, with a central island that might have served as our supper salad, contained a fountain of his construction. When one set a small mill in motion and removed a cork from a pipe, it played with sufficient force to wet the back of one’s hand quite thoroughly.

To my mind this curious falsehood had been told with remarkable simplicity and beauty; but I had heard it only once, and that alters matters. Doubtless the others had enjoyed it when it was new.

Sir Dinadan the Humorist awoke first, and presently woke everybody else with a practical joke of a decidedly shabby sort. He fastened several metal mugs to a dog’s tail and let the creature loose. Frantic with terror, it raced round and round the place, pursued by the roaring pack of other dogs, who collided and crashed into whatever lay before them, producing utter confusion and a deafening uproar. Every man and woman there laughed until the tears ran down; some tumbled from their chairs and rolled upon the floor in transports of delight. They might all have been children. Sir Dinadan took such pride in his achievement that he could not resist explaining, again and again until it grew tiresome, just how that immortal inspiration had struck him. Like humorists of his particular sort, he went on laughing long after everyone else had finished. So elated was he that he resolved to deliver a speech—a humorous speech, naturally. Never, I think, have I heard so many exhausted old jokes threaded together. He surpassed the minstrels in badness, surpassed even the circus clown. It was a singularly melancholy thing to sit there, thirteen hundred years before my birth, and hear again those feeble, stale, worm-eaten jokes that had given me stomach cramps as a boy thirteen hundred years later. It nearly persuaded me that a new joke could not possibly exist. Everybody laughed at these relics, but then everybody always does; I had observed that several centuries afterwards. The scoffer, of course, did not laugh—by which I mean the boy. He scoffed instead; nothing escaped his scorn. Most of Sir Dinadan’s jokes, he declared, were rotten, and the remainder petrified. I approved of ‘petrified,’ believing myself that only geological periods could properly express the majestic antiquity of certain specimens. But this pretty conceit found no lodging in the boy’s mind, since geology was not invented yet. Still, I noted the remark down, intending, if I survived, to educate the commonwealth until it appreciated it. There is no sense in discarding a good thing merely because its market is not yet ready.

Then Sir Kay stood up and began stoking his history-mill, using me as its fuel.

‘So you believe your master really was bitten by the beetle, and that the bite made him ill?’

‘I don’t believe anything about it—I know. Why would he dream so much about gold if that gold bug hadn’t bitten him? I’ve heard about those gold bugs before.’

‘But how can you tell he dreams about gold?’

‘How can I tell? Because he talks about it in his sleep—that’s how I know.’

‘Well, Jup, perhaps you are right. But what happy circumstance has brought me the honour of your visit today?’

‘What do you mean, master?’

‘Did Mr. Legrand send a message with you?’

‘No, master. I brought this letter here.’ Jupiter handed me a note, which read:

‘MY DEAR —— Why have you stayed away so long? I hope you have not been foolish enough to take offense at some small abruptness of mine; but no, that seems unlikely. Since we last met I have had serious reasons for anxiety. There is something I must tell you, though I hardly know how to explain it, or whether I should explain it at all.

‘I have been unwell for several days, and poor old Jup’s well-intentioned attentions irritate me almost beyond endurance. Can you believe it? The other day he had a huge stick ready to punish me for slipping away from him and spending the day alone in the mainland hills. I truly believe that only my sickly appearance saved me from a beating.

‘I have added nothing to my collection since we met.

‘If you can possibly arrange it, come back with Jupiter. Please come. I want to see you tonight about an important matter. I assure you, it is of the very highest importance.

‘Ever yours, WILLIAM LEGRAND.’

Something in the note’s tone made me deeply uneasy. Its entire style was markedly unlike Legrand’s usual writing. What could he be imagining? What new obsession had taken hold of his excitable mind? What possible ‘matter of the highest importance’ could he have to deal with? Jupiter’s account did not suggest anything good. I feared that the constant weight of misfortune had finally disturbed my friend’s reason. Without hesitating, I therefore prepared to go with the Black man.

When we reached the wharf, I noticed a scythe and three spades, all apparently new, lying in the bottom of the boat we were to take.

‘What is all this for, Jup?’
